extracted.intended_audience: administrative analysts, public administrators, management planners, and office/unit heads
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on scheduling, progress reporting, and management control techniques for administrative organizations, including use of unit production charts, limits of central control, and environmental factors affecting administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular progress reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress is reported at regular intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a percentage scale (0–100) showing percentage of work completed and time elapsed (two color strips for scheduled work). In central offices supervisors inspect with employees to determine progress; field workers may mail weekly coupons showing units completed. Periodic photographic reports of job cards (using cardboard masks with standardized headings) inform administrative officials of exact project status and available employees for assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit Production Chart as condensed control information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the administrative analyst a condensed 'Unit Production Chart' indicating capacity and expected volume of work for each unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chart should indicate capacity in man-hours by occupational classification and volume expected during the production period. Professional/technical units usually cover individual workloads; clerical offices may treat groups of identical positions as a whole. Unit heads should size up progress at regular intervals and send properly filled charts at stated intervals to the central scheduling official.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and graphical representation of charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make charts simple by eliminating detailed data and expressing time and work graphically by bar lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color schemes to differentiate classes of work (recurrent, special, ordinary, rush). If individual task assignment records exist, the chart should summarize job cards. Assign numbers to each administrative sequence/major task (entered both on unit's card file and central schedule). Lump small routine jobs together under a standard symbol and include allowance for unpredictable work, visitors, correspondence, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance submission and tentative future charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit heads should send production charts sufficiently in advance and, if possible, a tentative chart for the following period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance charts allow the analyst to assign work equal to vacant work-hours shown. Tentative future charts help anticipate assignments further ahead and identify need for extra personnel, overtime, or postponement. Avoid scheduling up to the limit to allow leeway for time-estimate errors, unexpected work, and 'breathing spells'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active co-operation and confirmation of time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The analyst must secure active co-operation of officials who will perform or supervise work; time estimates must be confirmed by operating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary schedules should be prepared as far in advance as possible and circulated to participating offices, carrying statements of objectives and methods, sequence outlines, and tentative job times and dates. Unit heads should confirm or amend initial estimates and suggest necessary specification changes; returned papers form the basis for definite scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and circulation of a definite schedule with job tickets
rubrics_metrics.description: After review and agreement make a definite schedule, obtain necessary approval, circulate it, and distribute job tickets to be returned as tasks are completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lengthy tasks may have intermediate tickets indicating 25%, 50%, 75% completion. The analyst posts data from incoming tickets on the schedule to obtain a running record of progress. Clerical scheduling work can be delegated where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel presentation of estimated and actual job times
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange schedules so estimated and actual job times and completion dates run in parallel columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits easy focus on work behind schedule and helps assemble production-meeting agendas. Unit heads should report errors in time estimates at meetings so current schedules can be revised and experience used in future scheduling. Completed schedules serve to record relative success, analyze deficiencies, support budget estimates, reallocate personnel, and aid administrative cost accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reserve personnel and exchange service integrated with scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate a pool of reserve personnel and an exchange service with the scheduling process to increase flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These services help keep unit capacities commensurate with current workloads and apply organizational resources where most needed, enhancing flexibility without disadvantages of strict functionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly minute management control (limits of control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Management control practiced too minutely will defeat its purpose; avoid central scheduling of intra-divisional business or minor small tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group small routine tasks under 'routine' and allow unit heads to include them in production charts. Scheduling of standardized recurrent sequences is semi-automatic—fit standard sequences with non-standard and routine work and notify appropriate units when projects will arrive. Proper allowances must be made for motion delay and backlog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine central scheduling to major, multi-office undertakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative analysts should generally confine scheduling and procedural control to larger undertakings requiring considerable effort by multiple offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include preparation of development plans, surveys, budget work, consummation of important deals, construction programs, important conferences, committee work, and liaison with outside organizations. Analysts should also be informed of or arrange such activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not usurp line assignment duties; keep informed and be diplomatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyst should not attempt to regulate assignment of work within units or closely integrated subdivisions—this is the duty of line officials and operating staff heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analyst should stay informed of unit activities, initiate or participate in eliminating duplication and unessential operations, and always be diplomatic—avoiding 'laying down the law.' Improvements should be initiated co-operatively so operating officials receive due credit; if pressure is necessary, apply it through the administrator and seldom directly by the analyst.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scheduling records for learning and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use returned schedules and reports of estimate mistakes to revise current schedules and improve future scheduling technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completed schedules and unit production charts provide material for analyzing deficiencies, improving technique, supporting budget estimates, reapportioning personnel, and administrative cost accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt scientific-management principles prudently in administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a rational, scientific technique of administration by standardizing data, observing, and analyzing, but recognize limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where exact factual knowledge is lacking, use inferential logic; administrative tasks are harder to measure than directly productive work, require leeway for the unpredictable, and involve relationships between individuals and groups. Convert conceptual devices (functions, units, concentration, devolution) into practical classification tools and develop techniques of measuring and comparing while accepting that administration may not become an exact science overnight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify and respond to environmental factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Take account of four major environmental groups—physical, political, legal, and socio-psychological—when planning and deciding whether to bend policies or seek to change the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each stage weigh which approach is appropriate (abandon an unpopular activity, try to sell it, plan in terms of legal status quo, or seek new legislation). Administration largely consists of responding to environmental stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider physical environment when designing administrative structure and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical problems determine the subject, objectives, and techniques of administration and set up necessities of administration (e.g., required personnel types and coordination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic concentration, uniformity of operating conditions, and convenient channels of information permit centralized, functionalized organizations with elaborate staff offices; dispersed activities and variable conditions call for decentralization and semi-autonomy. Communication problems strongly influence administrative structure and procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and manage political influences in administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Program planning is essentially political and organizations should develop and coordinate policy-forming opinion among employees; administrators must weigh outside and internal political pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators cannot always follow purely technical economy/efficiency; they must listen to political advisors who monitor public reaction. Political consequences may justify cumbersome procedures (e.g., graft precautions). Distinguish legitimate from illegitimate political pressure in light of communal political ethos, and respond sympathetically to 'proper' requests while refusing 'improper' ones—bearing in mind the distinction is often unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precisely define functions and align responsibility with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Each function and activity should be precisely defined and allocated, with responsibility and authority running parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy is desirable internally, though sometimes organizations must use bureaucratic 'run-around' tactics to deflect undue external pressures; such tactics can protect the organization but may be abused to hide error or indolence.
